item.title: Kimwolf v7 Hides DDoS Traffic Behind Chrome Fingerprints and Ethereum
item.description:
Kimwolf v7 Android TV botnet adds Chrome-fingerprinted HTTP/2 floods and Ethereum ENS C2 resolution, making attack traffic and infrastructure harder to block than any prior version.
Key details:
- C2 resilience is now three-tier: Ethereum ENS queried across five shuffled public RPC endpoints (including a suspected operator facade at eth.rpcuniverse[.]com), then a Tor .onion backup, then a local proxy on 127.0.0.1:23075. All three were added directly in response to December 2025 takedowns. Blocking any single RPC node is ineffective.
- The new HTTP/2 flood uses the nghttp2 library to construct full Chrome browser fingerprints at the protocol and header level, defeating fingerprint-based DDoS mitigations. A UDP flood with ARM NEON SIMD acceleration targets the specific processors in Android TV hardware.
- Initial access abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) on port 5555, tunneled through residential proxy services, no authentication required. The bot masquerades as "netd_service" and eight APKs disguised as "SystemService" probed for root between October and December 2025.
- Scale is significant: roughly 1.8 million infected devices, 1.7 billion DDoS commands issued in three days, and a linked 31.4 Tbps peak attack in November 2025. Unit 42 clustered 22 C2 IPs in Saint Petersburg sharing one SSH host key.

item.title: Largest AI Supply Chain Breach of 2026: LiteLLM Hack Impacts Thousands of Global Enterprises – Claim Your Ethical Disclosure
item.description:
TeamPCP's AI supply chain attack hit LiteLLM via a poisoned Trivy CI/CD pipeline, silently exfiltrating secrets from 2,488 enterprises. A 153GB raw dump confirms AWS, Cisco, Samsung, Siemens, and Boeing among victims.
- TeamPCP first compromised the GitHub Actions pipeline for Trivy, a popular open-source vulnerability scanner. Because LiteLLM used Trivy in its own CI/CD pipeline, attackers inherited legitimate runner access and stole LiteLLM's PyPI publishing tokens, then pushed malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8.
- Payload delivery used a .pth Python startup hook, executing the moment the Python interpreter initialized regardless of whether LiteLLM was imported. The three-stage payload harvested environment variables, .kube/config, .aws/credentials, attempted Kubernetes lateral movement, and installed a persistent systemd backdoor masquerading as "System Telemetry Service."
- Hudson Rock obtained the raw 153GB RAR archive: 433,909 files, 118,829 CI runner dumps attributed to 2,488 corporate domains. Exposed secrets include AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, SALESFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET, SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, Azure tokens, and AI provider API keys, many in plain text.
Inspect site-packages directories for unauthorized .pth files and audit systemd services for masquerading entries. Rotate all cloud IAM keys, Kubernetes tokens, and VCS PATs that touched any LiteLLM environment. Review AWS CloudTrail and Kubernetes API audit logs from March 24, 2026 onward.

item.title: Lazarus Used Post-Quantum Key Exchange to Deliver Zero-Day
item.description:
North Korea 🇰🇵's Lazarus group deployed a Windows kernel zero-day via a post-quantum encrypted channel against defense and aerospace firms in France 🇫🇷, Germany 🇩🇪, Brazil 🇧🇷, and India 🇮🇳, with a patch shipping August 11.
- CVE-2026-68820 is a use-after-free race condition in AFD.sys, the Windows kernel socket driver, flagged by Microsoft as actively exploited in the wild. Check Point reported it July 28; the patch landed August 12 Patch Tuesday. Prioritize this one.
- The exploit arrived through a layered crypto handshake: MISTPEN (an in-memory downloader using Microsoft Graph API and attacker-controlled OneDrive files for C2) loaded a fingerprinting module that negotiated Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange with the operator, then decrypted the payload in memory over GOST-CBC on top of AES. No exploit touches disk.
- What landed was FudModule v3.1, Lazarus's kernel rootkit. It kills 94 ETW providers, removes minifilters, disables telemetry callbacks, wipes the NT Kernel Logger, and now tampers with Smart App Control by resetting policy state and forcing a code integrity reload.
- Infrastructure ran through compromised Roundcube servers (CVE-2025-49113) and PrestaShop sites hosting RelayShell, a new PHP webshell passing traffic via session files across at least 17 relay servers. Three fake Enveil sites distributed Troy, a new backdoor with 17 operator commands, via a trojanized PDF viewer.
Patch AFD.sys immediately.

item.title: Blacklight: Illuminating AI Agent Artifacts for Attackers and Defenders
item.description:
SpecterOps releases Blacklight, an open-source toolkit mapping AI agent artifacts across Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, and Antigravity CLI as a new post-exploitation surface on developer endpoints.
- Auth files like .codex/auth.json and .claude/.credentials.json hold access tokens, refresh tokens, OAuth metadata, and tenant identifiers. Claude Code's settings.json can expose API keys and cloud credentials in environment variables. These artifacts support direct session impersonation, not just credential confirmation.
- Session transcripts, workspace metadata, MCP server configs, and SQLite chat databases (.cursor/chats/**/store.db, .gemini/antigravity-cli/conversations/*.db) consolidate internal hostnames, repo names, deployment procedures, and infrastructure references into a single collection target.
- Blacklight Scout ships as a Windows BOF (ai_path_scout.x64.o), macOS dylib, and Linux shared object. The loaders enumerate artifact paths and rank collection candidates without reading file bodies, preserving OPSEC. Deeper on-host analysis runs via ai_path_scout-windows-x64.exe or the managed .NET executable.
- For defenders, the toolkit provides osquery configs for artifact inventory and file_events monitoring, plus PowerShell scripts to enable Windows Security Event 4663 with SACL-based file-read auditing on high-value paths. Provider compliance APIs (OpenAI Compliance Platform, Claude Compliance Activity Feed) offer off-host visibility.

item.title: WS-Trust Autologon Endpoint: Password Spray Without Smart Lockout Blocking
item.description:
Legacy Entra ID WS-Trust autologon endpoint bypasses Smart Lockout entirely, confirms valid passwords on MFA-protected accounts, and leaves near-zero trace in standard sign-in logs.
Key findings:
- The endpoint autologon.microsoftazuread-sso[.]com/{tenant}/winauth/trust/2005/usernamemixed accepts plaintext credentials via SOAP and returns AADSTS error codes that distinguish a wrong password from a correct one blocked by MFA or Conditional Access. Codes AADSTS50055, AADSTS50076, and AADSTS53003 all confirm the password was accepted before a downstream control intervened.
- Smart Lockout never fired during testing. Over 1,000 spray attempts against a single account from one unfamiliar IP produced no AADSTS50053 lockout response and no backoff. The account signed in normally afterward.
- Failed attempts do not appear in standard Entra ID sign-in logs. The Unified Audit Log does capture traffic to this endpoint, making UAL the only log source that exposes the spray.
- Confirmed MFA-protected passwords remain useful post-spray: adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device code flow abuse, and primary refresh token theft can all complete the sign-in without MFA interaction.
Remediation priority: disable the usernamemixed endpoint at the tenant level if no Office 2013 pre-May-2015 clients exist, then block legacy authentication via Conditional Access policy.

item.title: Abuse of alternative runtime environments Deno-tes defender headaches
item.description:
Threat cluster abuses Deno JavaScript runtime as a fileless execution engine across multiple victims in early 2026, combining ClickFix lures, SEO poisoning, and MSI staging to deliver in-memory C2 payloads and evade conventional detection.
Key findings:
- Attack chain is consistent across all four victims: ClickFix lure or web-triggered PowerShell drops a malicious MSI via msiexec, which deploys VBS and PowerShell loaders to %LocalAppData%\Serial\, then downloads the legitimate Deno runtime using curl.exe and tar.exe before executing a Base64-encoded JavaScript payload entirely in memory using the -A (allow-all) flag. No script ever touches disk at the JS stage.
- The JavaScript payload fingerprints the host (username, hostname, memory, OS release), uses localhost port 10044 as a pseudo-mutex, beacons to C2 /health endpoints to check campaign status, then retrieves secondary payloads from /mv2/ and executes them in-memory. JWT tokens embedded in requests carry custom campaignId and campaignName fields, suggesting a MaaS infrastructure model.
- In case 4, the MSI was "PsExec.msi" (SHA256: 74260ef8c440692043aaa4656947258b3acfc207c95f09682b69d031b42890a0) served from a spoofed GitHub repo via poisoned Bing results. Persistence lands at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Papa_software10 calling wscript.exe on Lynx_system59.vbs. Post-compromise included SYSTEM-level shell via PsExec, domain enumeration, and SAM hive credential dumping.

item.title: ClickFix campaign abuses Deno runtime for infostealer delivery
item.description:
ClickFix campaign uses Deno JavaScript runtime to deliver a Python-based infostealer across 500+ compromised WordPress sites, blending LOLBin abuse with legitimate tooling to evade detection.
Key details:
- Attack chain: Cloudflare-themed ClickFix lures on compromised WordPress sites inject malicious JS referencing columbnezhjdq[.]com/goolgetagmanager[.]js. Users are prompted to run a clipboard PowerShell command that drops an MSI, which writes november85.cmd and Griffin20.ps1 to AppData, then uses winget.exe to install the legitimate Deno runtime before fetching remote JS from webstizkgao[.]com.
- Deno acts as the orchestrator post-install: running additional PowerShell, conducting recon, and establishing persistence via registry Run keys invoking JS through a headless conhost.exe process. C2 later pivoted to ordinary-computer-analytical-spell.trycloudflare[.]com, storing stage content in a registry key disguised as a Microsoft Edge update.
- The Python-based infostealer (install.pyc), pulled from 162.33.177[.]16 and executed via pythonw.exe, harvests browser data, crypto wallet contents, and keystrokes.
- Over 500 WordPress sites were identified hosting the injection. Columbnezhjdq[.]com was registered June 1, 2026, two days before the campaign began.
Hunt for deno.exe executing from user-writable directories, conhost.exe with unusual parent processes, and Run key persistence invoking JS. Full IOC list and Sophos detection rules are in the report.

item.title: Russian-Linked Hackers Accessed Polish Power Plant OT Network Through Private APN, Says CERT.PL
item.description:
Sandworm-linked actors forced a Polish 🇵🇱 CHP plant turbine and water treatment shutdown by pivoting through a private APN, the first documented OT intrusion via this vector.
- Initial access came through a compromised FortiGate VPN/firewall at a wind farm. Attackers then pivoted via a Teltonika cellular router over SSH to a private APN managed by a distribution system operator, reaching OT assets that operators assumed were isolated.
- A WAGO PFC200 PLC with default admin credentials was exposed on the APN web interface. After owning it, actors SSH'd into the plant OT network, found three Siemens PLCs, set them to STOP mode, and password-locked them to block recovery. Steam turbine and water treatment both went offline.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and layered: logs destroyed, Moxa network devices sabotaged, WAGO controller physically damaged, Teltonika router factory-reset, and FortiGate restored to defaults, erasing the pivot path.
- Part of the broader Sandworm December 2025 campaign hitting 30 Polish 🇵🇱 renewable energy facilities and a second CHP plant on Dec 29-30, 2025. Post-mortem took three months due to evidence destruction.
Takeaway: Audit every private APN as an untrusted network segment. Hunt for SSH tunnels from cellular routers into OT. Default credentials on PLC web interfaces are the kill shot here. CERT.PL recommendations and full report are published.

item.title: CERT Polska exposes multi-stage cyberattack on energy infrastructure involving VPN, private APN, OT network tunneling
item.description:
CERT Polska exposes a novel private APN pivot used to tunnel from a compromised wind farm into a CHP plant's OT network, shutting down a steam turbine and water treatment system on Dec. 29, 2025.
- Initial access: FortiGate VPN concentrators at wind farm substations were internet-exposed with no MFA. The attacker pivoted to a Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router, used SSH tunneling into a private APN, and discovered a WAGO PFC200 PLC configured with default admin credentials. SSH was then enabled via the web interface and used as the OT network gateway into the CHP plant, a vector CERT Polska says has no prior known precedent.
- Dec. 18-25 reconnaissance: the attacker scanned the APN for VNC, HTTP, S7, and Modbus services, made manual RDP credential attempts, and on Dec. 25 connected to three Siemens PLCs (S7-300, S7-1200, S7-1500) via S7 protocol, likely staging for disruption.
- Dec. 29 impact: starting at 05:30, the attacker switched all three Siemens PLCs to STOP mode, password-locked them, reconfigured seven Moxa serial servers and three Moxa switches with unreachable IPs (127.0.0.1), and halted cogeneration. Recovery teams were still restoring systems while the attacker remained active.
- Forensic loss: the WAGO PLC had its partition table corrupted by the attacker before exit. Factory resets of the Teltonika router and FortiGate destroyed remaining logs. PLC restoration wiped controller logs permanently, confirmed by Siemens.

item.title: Head Mare APT Group exploits vulnerabilities in unpatched TrueConf server to deliver PhantomCore malware to conference participants
item.description:
Head Mare APT trojanizes TrueConf installers via server-side RCE to deliver PhantomCore to every conference participant, including employees of unaffected organizations who join external meetings.
Key details:
- Two unpatched vulnerabilities (KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058) in TrueConf Server, exploitable via port 4307/TCP on all versions since 2022, let Head Mare execute code as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, drop a web shell at C:\Program Files\TrueConf Server\httpconf\site\public\js\locale.php, and replace the legitimate x64 client installer at ClientInstFiles\trueconf_windows_client_x64.exe. Patches landed June 18, 2026 in versions 5.3.9, 5.4.9, and 5.5.5.
- PhantomCore (MD5: c5a460e4e68a088f6e51b2c6474642ec) drops to %LOCALAPPDATA%\TrueConf\Client\api-ms-win-crt-time-l1-1-0-2.dll and persists via COM hijack at HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{0340F119-A598-4ed9-B0AC-6F6A12D3E755}\InprocServer32. A two-component backdoor (SysExcSvc and SysReadSvc services) uses Microsoft OneDrive for C2; on Linux, a separate backdoor uses GitHub as its C2 channel.
- Supply-chain blast radius extends beyond TrueConf server owners: any employee who joined a meeting on a compromised server and clicked the update prompt is potentially infected, making participant-side hunting mandatory.
Hunt for the COM hijack key, SysExcSvc/SysReadSvc services, and api-ms-win-crt-time-l1-1-0-2.dll in the TrueConf client path.

item.title: Gone with the WindRelay: A New Malware Combo Behind a Growing Fraud Scheme
item.description:
WindRelay, a new NFC relay malware, pairs with SpyNote RAT to drain victims twice in one 13-minute call: a digital loan plus live card-present purchases, all without screen sharing.
Key findings:
- The attack chain is three layers in one session. A vishing call posing as a bank employee guides the victim to sideload SpyNote (T1476), labeled with the victim's own name to kill hesitation. SpyNote's Accessibility Service abuse then silently pushes WindRelay onto the device, no victim interaction needed. The fraudster used dual payout channels before the bank could react: a loan taken via remote access to the banking app, then physical transactions via relayed NFC.
- WindRelay's permission set is purpose-engineered: NFC for live card capture, INTERNET/ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE for real-time relay to a fraudster-held terminal, READ_CONTACTS for next-target harvesting, an unusual DUMP permission for device inspection, and custom apk-scoped permissions to resist security tooling inspection.
- Group-IB found 23 WindRelay samples on VirusTotal between November 2025 and July 2026, targeting Czechia, Slovakia 🇸🇰, and Slovenia, with some carrying victim-personalized labels. Four C2 IPs are confirmed: 88.86.124[.]114, 185.100.87[.]116, 185.100.87[.]223, and 213.218.160[.]48.
- Detection gap: screen-share absence does not mean no remote access. SpyNote achieves full device control through Accessibility Services alone, bypassing common fraud-monitoring triggers.

item.title: Deleting the Defenders: A Commodity BYOVD Toolkit That Erases Host Safeguards
item.description:
Commodity BYOVD toolkit "Saked" delivered via WinRAR SFX archives wipes 281 files across Defender, 9+ AV vendors, backups, and recovery data before dropping a follow-on payload. Static detection misses it entirely.
Key findings:
- The dropper is a WinRAR SFX that extracts 7z.exe, cecho.exe, nircmd.exe, and a password-protected same.zip (password: stucha, Russian 🇷🇺 slang) to %TEMP%\saked, then runs a randomly named batch script. The script detects Defender and Windows Security services via tasklist and reg query, disables Windows Update (wuauserv, dosvc, bits, UsoSvc, WaaSMedicSvc via sc.exe config start= disabled), then launches mika.exe (SHA-256 9163d413..., compiled 2025-10-17, first seen 2026-02-08) with /DelWD. Static pivots on the shared imphash 12e12319... or Rich-header hash 5a0b7a24... return the entire commodity WinRAR SFX population, not this family.
- The BYOVD path: mika.exe unpacks genuine IObit Unlocker 1.6.0.16 (IObitUnlocker.exe SHA-256 eaa9dc1c..., IObitUnlocker.sys SHA-256 1845fe85...) to %TEMP%\IObitUnlocker and issues one IObitUnlocker.exe /Delete /Advanced command targeting 281 paths. The driver opens \\.\IObitUnlockerDevice, receives IOCTL 0x222124 (CVE-2020-14974, CVE-2020-14975), calls ZwTerminateProcess on any non-safe-listed process holding a target file, then force-deletes it from kernel mode, including live Defender services. A runtime mutex "Unlocker by Eject NotOfficial" marks Saked's execution.

item.title: Fake CCleaner installs GhostDesk Chrome spyware
item.description:
Fake CCleaner installer drops GhostDesk, a Chrome extension spyware that keyloggs, harvests credentials, steals cookies, and captures screenshots via a WebSocket C2 chain.
Key findings:
- Initial access is a typosquat site, ccleanerwind[.]top, serving a fake CCleaner.exe (SHA256: c0b4a4af...b9ce23). The binary's internal name svc_it7p and original filename rt_mxk.exe betray the impersonation. The same CScript-based loader also delivers fake 7-Zip and Adobe Acrobat variants, all phoning home to the same C2.
- The loader drops a legitimate cscript.exe, uses it to run scripts that query the machine GUID, write a reflexive loader to %AppData%\Microsoft\DriverStore\runtimebroker.dll, and patch Chrome's Security Extension manifest.json to add background.js and content.js from %LocalAppData%\cse.
- C2 is established via a local WebSocket on 192.168.100.4:49727 bridged to liderongrade.duckdns[.]org:4444 (IP: 193.169.240[.]81). background.js maintains a secondary relay at 127.0.0.1:7345/ext for in-browser exfiltration of cookies, screenshots, and keystrokes.
- content.js keyloggs input fields, intercepts POST/submit form data for credential and financial keywords, performs clipboard hijacking for crypto addresses, and injects arbitrary scripts into targeted pages.
Takeaway: Hunt for unsigned or recently modified DLLs at %AppData%\Microsoft\DriverStore\runtimebroker.dll and inspect Chrome's Security Extension manifest.json for unexpected service worker entries.

item.title: CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard Weaponizes Hotel Wi-Fi Captive Portals to Steal Microsoft 365 Credentials

Victims connecting to Wi-Fi hit AitM redirects via three paths: M365 credential phishing, device code/OAuth phishing that registers the attacker's session in Entra ID and bypasses conventional MFA, or ClickFix fake-update lures (fake Windows Update, Defender, DirectX, browser prompts) that trick users into running commands that drop CornFlake and ChocoShell. IOCs include ms365-device[.]com, ms365-live[.]com, m365-owa[.]com, owa-ms365[.]com, and AitM IPs 31.57.243[.]154 and 104.194.159[.]150.
- CornFlake (Go-based RAT, SHA-256: 918fa52a...) drops to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe, persists via service registration, Registry Run keys, scheduled tasks, and a watchdog, and uses ECDH P-256 encrypted C2. ChocoShell (PowerShell stealer, SHA-256: be998574...) runs in-memory, disables AMSI via .NET reflection, UAC-bypasses via SilentCleanup/wsreset/sdclt hijacks, then harvests browser cookies (ChromeKatz-derived), Firefox NSS decryption, Chrome DevTools Protocol, M365/Azure WAM Token Broker cache, and Wi-Fi creds via netsh wlan.

item.title: Tracking Shai-Hulud: Inside the ChainDrop NPM Worm
item.description:
ChainDrop npm worm poisons 400+ packages in under 4 hours by hijacking a maintainer's GitHub account, abusing trusted CI/CD pipelines to publish packages with valid SLSA Build Level 3 attestations, and anchoring C2 in an Ethereum smart contract.
- TeamPCP's ChainDrop (a Shai-Hulud variant) entered npm on August 4, 2026 via a compromised keyv maintainer account. The attacker pushed setup.mjs and Math_Symbol.js to main branches and modified package.json to add a preinstall hook. Because the attacker operated as the legitimate maintainer, the existing GitHub Actions pipeline built and published keyv 6.0.0 with valid OIDC trusted-publisher provenance and SLSA Build L3 attestation. Signed provenance did not equal safe content.
- Math_Symbol.js runs under the Bun runtime (downloaded at v1.3.13) deliberately to bypass EDRs monitoring Node.js child-process behavior. It harvests npm tokens, GitHub PATs, OIDC tokens, AWS/GCP/Azure credentials, Kubernetes configs (~/.kube/config), HashiCorp Vault tokens (VAULT_TOKEN), SSH keys, and Claude Code/Copilot configs. Stolen data is AES-256-GCM encrypted, RSA-4096 key-wrapped, and exfiltrated to attacker-created GitHub repos (description: "Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again"). Fallback C2 via EtherHiding: Ethereum contract 0xE1f2395ee43e45A1556EC6438a88c31B83493103 delivers live domains, making blocklists ineffective.

item.title: Bird Watching: Characterizing the Infrastructure and Behavior of Falcon-branded Extortion Operations

item.title: Threat Hunting Case Study: The Gentlemen
item.description:

item.title: Bypassing Android Hardware Attestation from the Analyst's Chair
item.description:
Android hardware attestation relayed, not broken: Quarkslab shows how a Frida hook and a clean burner phone flip a backend verdict from rejected to valid without touching crypto or firmware.
Key findings:
- The attestation chain's RootOfTrust (tag [704] in hardwareEnforced) is what kills analysis on a rooted device. verifiedBootState reports Unverified and deviceLocked is false because those values are written by secure hardware before Android boots, no userspace patch changes them. The relay sidesteps this entirely by having a stock, locked phone generate the chain instead.
- The seam is KeystoreAttestation.generateAttestedKey(challenge: ByteArray). Frida hooks that single method, re-encodes the raw challenge bytes as unpadded base64url, ships it to the clean oracle device via HTTP POST /attest, and returns the resulting AttestedKey to the app. The local Keystore is never called. The app forwards a genuine chain it believes is its own.
- The backend cannot distinguish a relayed chain from a local one. KeyDescription carries no field binding the attestation to a transport session, network address, or process. The nonce (attestationChallenge) is the only freshness signal, and the relay forwards it untouched.
- The decisive mitigation is one backend comparison: read attestationApplicationId (tag [709], softwareEnforced) and reject any chain whose package name or signing certificate SHA-256 digest does not match the expected app.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Microsoft SharePoint JWT Token Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-55040)

- Android core evidence lives in /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/: wa.db (contacts, phone numbers, display names) and msgstore.db (messages, timestamps, status, media references). Root or a physical image is required to read them directly. Encrypted backups at /data/media/0/WhatsApp/Databases/msgstore.db.cryptXX need the key from /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/ to decrypt.
- Shared prefs and registration XMLs in /data/data/com.whatsapp/shared_prefs/ expose account phone number, display name, and app version. axolotl.db holds Signal/Double Ratchet cryptographic keys and account identifiers.
- On iOS, ChatStorage.sqlite under AppDomainGroup-group.net.whatsapp.WhatsApp.shared is the primary target. Tables ZWAMESSAGE and ZWAMEDIAITEM carry message records and attachment metadata. ContactsV2.sqlite, BackedUpKeyValue.sqlite, and blockedcontacts.dat round out the account picture.

item.title: A Deep Dive into LNK Files | Windows Forensics
item.description:
LNK files outlive deleted originals: Windows shortcut metadata records file interaction, source location, and device identity long after the target file disappears.
- LNK files are auto-created without user action when files are opened via File Explorer or Open/Save dialogs. Primary locations are C:\Users\<Username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent and the Office equivalent under AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Office\Recent. They persist even after the original file is deleted, moved, or unplugged.
- Each LNK contains two distinct timestamp sets: source timestamps (the shortcut itself) and target timestamps (the original file). If target Created is newer than target Modified, the file was likely copied or moved, not originally created there. Conflating the two is a common analytical error.
- Volume serial number, volume label, drive type, UNC path, and machine name inside the LNK let you correlate removable-media access to USB registry artifacts without the drive being present. A LNK pointing to a removable drive cross-referenced with ShellBags and Jump Lists can identify the exact device and the folders browsed on it.
- Attackers weaponize LNK files by embedding PowerShell or other commands in the target path and command-line arguments fields, disguising malicious execution as a legitimate shortcut. Examine those fields during malware triage.

CrowdStrike catalogs 21 ESX shell obfuscation techniques spanning Unicode injection, cryptographic ciphers, and infrastructure-keyed payloads, with CQL detection patterns for all six categories.
- ESX logs capture commands at parse time, before shell expansion. That gap means $(printf "\x65\x73\x78\x63\x6c\x69") system syslog config get executes as esxcli but logs as hex, defeating any keyword search. Groups including SCATTERED SPIDER, BlackBasta, Akira, and Royal have already demonstrated they move fast once they reach the hypervisor layer.
- CrowdStrike validated 21 techniques across six categories on ESX 7.0.3: escape sequence encoding (octal/hex printf, ANSI-C quoting), string manipulation (awk chr generation, env variable harvesting, reversal via sed/od), invisible Unicode injection (Zero-Width Space through SPUA characters, over 131k codepoints available), cryptographic schemes (XOR, Fibonacci keystream, affine cipher, CBC-like chaining), infrastructure-keyed payloads (build number or hostname length as XOR key, multi-conditional gates), and alternative encodings (Morse code, binary, scientific notation). Maps to T1027, T1059.004, and T1140.
- Infrastructure-keyed payloads are the highest-risk finding: a payload XORed with the ESX build number or hostname length only decodes on the target host, breaking sandbox analysis entirely.

item.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in JetBrains TeamCity (CVE-2026-63077)
item.description:
CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity is a critical unauthenticated RCE via unsafe XStream deserialization, now confirmed exploited in the wild and added to CISA KEV on August 5, 2026. Patch to 2026.1.3 immediately.
- CVE-2026-63077 affects TeamCity through 2026.1.2. The root cause: XStreamHolder.setupSecurityIfNeeded() appended TeamCity's allowlist on top of XStream's default permissions rather than replacing them, leaving Map and Throwable hierarchies open. The patch inserts xstream.addPermission(NoTypePermission.NONE) before populating the allowlist, making it deny-by-default.
- Attack chain requires two unauthenticated HTTP requests: POST to /app/agents/v1/register to obtain a session ID, then POST a crafted XML gadget chain to /app/agents/v1/commands/error. The gadget routes through HSQLMetadataStorage$SchemaMismatchException, BasicDataSource, FreeMarker BooleanModel, and TiedMapEntry to invoke BasicDataSource.getConnection(), which executes attacker SQL that writes a .jspws webshell into TeamCity's webroot for code execution.
- Key forensic artifacts: teamcity-server.log will show ConversionException errors referencing freemarker.core._TemplateModelException, BasicDataSource wrapped into f.e.b.BooleanModel, and the path /linked-hash-map/entry[3]/set/org.apache.commons.collections.keyvalue.TiedMapEntry on POSTs to /app/agents/v1/commands/error. The javaLogging file will contain an HsqlException naming the dropped .jspws file path.

item.title: The security signal log tailing can't see: tracking npm cooldown removals with Elastic Agent
item.description:
Elastic Security Labs built a CEL-based Elastic Agent integration to detect silent removal of npm's min-release-age supply-chain cooldown setting from developer workstations, closing a gap filestream cannot see.
Key findings:
- npm's min-release-age setting (available since npm 11.10) maps directly to T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools). It blocks freshly published, potentially compromised packages from resolving during the highest-risk window. The danger is silent removal: a developer or script can delete the line from ~/.npmrc and filestream-based monitoring never fires because filestream only emits on append, not on content removal.
- The CEL integration snapshots every .npmrc on a 6-hour heartbeat, hashes the content, and marks cooldown.absent = true in the next snapshot when min-release-age is gone. An agent-side JavaScript processor strips registry auth tokens before any data leaves the host, so //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken lines never reach Elasticsearch.
- Three filestream failures drove the switch: files under 1024 bytes are silently held back by the default fingerprint identity (switch to native/inode), clean_inactive and ignore_older must both be set to get periodic re-emission, and removal events simply never arrive.
- The adoption dashboard requires a heartbeat model, not emit-on-change. One-shot events age out of the time window and make adoption appear to erode when the setting is still in place.

item.title: Researchers Discover Hidden Backdoor in 20 Router Models Allowing Remote Root Access
item.description:
A vendor-built backdoor named ENDLESSDOORS ships across 20 Zbtlink router models, granting unauthenticated remote root access via outbound connections that bypass firewalls entirely. No patch exists.
- ENDLESSDOORS is built on rctl, a dormant 2015 open-source tool. Two userland processes masquerade as kernel threads named kworker (unbracketed, with real memory footprints) and launch automatically at boot via an init script called skworker. The implant dials out, so NAT and perimeter firewalls offer zero protection.
- The protocol is deliberately minimal: the router sends a 39-byte hello containing a class label and its LAN MAC address, with no handshake, no key exchange, and no verification. The server responds with shell commands executed as uid 0 via popen(). The reserved string rctlbash opens a second connection to port 7001 and spawns a live /bin/sh pseudo-terminal root shell.
- Four C2 endpoints serve the entire affected fleet: zbtctl.epplink[.]net resolving to 47.100.190[.]96 (Alibaba Cloud), hardcoded IP 47.107.224[.]89 (Alibaba Cloud), online-string[.]com resolving to 45.32.81[.]152 (Vultr), and rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba[.]com resolving to 43.248.136[.]125 (Jiangsu Dongyun Cloud).
- Zbtlink markets hardware under Wiflyer, ZBT, and ZBTWiFi on Amazon, Alibaba, and Shopify. The vendor claims the backdoor was a maintenance feature limited to sample units, then quietly pulled firmware downloads, undermining that explanation.

item.title: When Agentic Glue Melts: Exploiting Cloudflare Code Mode and Workers
item.description:
Five memory-corruption bugs in workerd, the runtime behind Cloudflare Workers and Code Mode, enable cross-tenant secret theft and sandbox escape to host RCE. Two rated Critical by Cloudflare. Patched in production; self-hosted deployments must update to v1.20260619.1.
Key findings:
- The attack surface is workerd's JSG layer, the C++ glue marshaling JavaScript calls into native code. Unlike V8, JSG had almost no prior public scrutiny, and the objects it allocates land on the tcmalloc heap, outside both the V8 sandbox cage and memory-protection keys. That means a bug there is not boxed in the way a V8 bug would be. Check Point found five bugs: two UAFs (node:zlib deflateParams and HTMLRewriter AttributesIterator), two URLPattern out-of-bounds reads, and a KV SQL authorizer bypass leading to arbitrary deserialization of attacker-controlled bytes into workerd's internal structured-clone deserializer.
- Cross-tenant secret theft via URLPattern OOB: a nested capture group like /(ab(cde))/ causes V8 to report two capture groups while nameList holds only one name. The loop reads 24 bytes past the vector end, treats them as a kj::String, and dereferences ptr, returning bytes at an attacker-chosen address. Using tcmalloc free-list layout and VFS file buffers as stable in-place primitives, one Worker can sweep the shared heap and read another tenant's secrets (Bearer tokens, private keys) without touching the cage or MPK-protected pages.

item.title: OctLurk and SilkLurk: Analysis of a Modular Cyber Espionage Framework
item.description:
Chinese-linked espionage campaign deploys two undocumented backdoors, OctLurk and SilkLurk, against government and public-sector targets across Central Asia and the Middle East, with Afghanistan and Syria also in scope.
Key findings:
- OctLurk and SilkLurk are modular backdoors sharing a plugin-based architecture that allows operators to extend capability post-compromise. Both use victim-specific decryption keys and heavy obfuscation, meaning a sample pulled from one victim will not decrypt cleanly on another, complicating bulk sandbox analysis.
- In-memory execution is central to both families, reducing on-disk footprint and making traditional file-hash hunting unreliable. Responders should prioritize memory forensics and look for anomalous injected modules in trusted processes.
- LurkProxy is a companion traffic-proxying utility used to route attacker C2 communications, obscuring true infrastructure. Network defenders should flag internal hosts making repeated, low-volume outbound connections to uncommon ports, consistent with proxy relay behavior.
- Targeted verticals include Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Law Enforcement, Healthcare, Research, and Logistics, indicating intelligence-collection intent rather than disruption. PlugX is listed as a related family, suggesting shared tooling or operator overlap with known Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage clusters.
Prioritize memory acquisition on compromised hosts before remediation.

item.title: ChainDrop: Inside a Self-Propagating npm Worm
item.description:
ChainDrop is a self-propagating npm worm that steals GitHub Actions runner secrets and uses Ethereum smart contracts for C2, marking a shift in supply chain attack sophistication.
- ChainDrop spreads by compromising npm packages and injecting malicious code that executes during install-time lifecycle hooks (postinstall), targeting any developer or CI/CD pipeline that installs an infected dependency.
- The worm targets GitHub Actions runner environments specifically, extracting secrets and tokens from the runner context, meaning a single poisoned dependency in a workflow can expose repository secrets, cloud credentials, and signing keys.
- C2 routing uses Ethereum smart contracts rather than hardcoded domains or IPs, making traditional domain-based blocklists and DNS sinkholes ineffective. The attacker updates the C2 endpoint by writing to the blockchain, and the malware reads it on-chain.
- For DFIR, key artifacts include postinstall scripts in package.json, unexpected outbound connections to Ethereum RPC endpoints from CI runners, and anomalous environment variable access (process.env) in Node.js child processes during build jobs.
Audit your npm dependency tree for unexpected postinstall hooks. In GitHub Actions, review runner logs for outbound calls to Ethereum JSON-RPC endpoints and treat any exposed GITHUB_TOKEN or cloud secret as fully compromised. IOC list and full technical details in the Unit 42 report.

item.title: UNC6671 Rebrands: Multi-Brand Vishing Extortion Targets Financial Services and Enterprise Cloud Environments
item.description:
UNC6671 did not retire with BlackFile: it rebranded across Redact, Pink, Helix, and Falcon, accelerating vishing-driven cloud extortion against financial services and private equity targets through mid-2026.
- UNC6671 calls employees on personal mobile numbers, spoofs legitimate helpdesk numbers, and directs victims to AiTM credential-harvesting subdomains (e.g., [company].createssopasskey[.]com, [company].addssopasskey[.]com) to steal M365 and Okta session tokens. Post-compromise, automated scripts exfiltrate SaaS data while operators delete password-reset confirmations, security alerts, and MFA-change notifications to suppress detection (T1070).
- Shared infrastructure ties all five brands together: passkeyhelpdesk[.]com targeted both Falcon and Helix victims simultaneously; setupsso[.]com and idokta[.]com bridged to BlackFile; passkeyms[.]com and mysecurepasskey[.]com bridged to Pink. Domain provisioning accelerated to one every 1.6 days in June-July 2026, with seven domains stood up in a 72-hour window July 20-22.
- Blockchain analysis of 18 BlackFile wallets from January-May 2026 shows 141.65 BTC received (~$10.69M USD). Final payments averaged $750K in over 53% of tracked cases, and payments continued past the May 11 "shutdown" announcement confirming rebranding was financial cover, not retirement.
- Hunt in Okta and Entra ID audit logs for system.multifactor.factor.setup events immediately preceded by user.authentication.auth_via_mfa failures.
